title: Your sitting
hook: bell, posture, breath, a closing wish of metta

segments.voice: Yesterday, nivarana: the five hindrances, visitors every sitter meets. Your line was name the visitor. Which one knocked most often? Day one hundred and sixteen, the last day with the breath.

For twenty days you've learned pieces. The four phrases. The sixteen steps. Counting. The visitors. Today we put them together into one thing you can actually do tomorrow morning, and the morning after, without this app, without a teacher, without anything but a place to sit. What helps is something simple and repeatable: ten minutes or twenty, done most days. Not a performance. Not a test. Just a habit with a shape to it. Today, you build yours.
screen: `TWENTY DAYS OF PIECES.` → `PUT THEM TOGETHER.` → `A HABIT WITH A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's a simple shape in four parts, drawn from the breathing discourse and from ordinary practice. First, a bell, or any clear beginning. In a monastery, a bell or gong may open the sitting; it marks the line between the rest of your day and this. A phone timer works fine. Second, posture. The breathing discourse says: sit down, fold the legs crosswise, set the body upright. That's the old ideal, but chairs and cushions both work. What matters is upright without stiffness: a straight back, relaxed shoulders, hands resting, eyes closed or softly lowered. Third, the breath. Use whatever you've learned. Count to ten if the mind is busy. Know the long and the short. Feel the whole body, kaya. When a visitor comes, name it, and come back. Don't try all sixteen steps at once. Pick one, and stay with it. Fourth, close with a wish of metta. Before you open your eyes, offer the phrases: to yourself, to someone you love, to everyone. May all beings be at ease. Some Buddhists end a sitting this way, sharing whatever good came of it outward. Then the bell again, and back to your day. How long? Ten minutes is a real sitting, and ten minutes on most days builds what an hour once a month can't: a habit. And look at the ten days behind you: sixteen steps, long and short, the whole body, joy and ease, the weather of the mind, gladdening, change, counting, the visitors, and now your own sitting. Ten minutes, yours.
screen: `A BELL: THE LINE BETWEEN.` · `UPRIGHT, NOT STIFF.` · `ONE STEP OF THE BREATH.` · `CLOSE WITH METTA.` · then, large: `TEN MINUTES, YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let's walk through it, shorter. The bell has just rung: that's your beginning. Now set your posture: upright, shoulders soft, hands resting. Take one step of the breath, whichever you like best: counting, long and short, or the whole body. Stay with it. When a visitor comes, name it, and return. Near the end, offer the phrases: may I be at ease, may all beings be at ease. Later today, if you can, try the full ten minutes. The bell holds the time.
Your sitting. Bell, posture, breath, and a closing wish of metta: a practice you can keep.
Your line: ten minutes, yours. Today or tomorrow morning, set a timer for ten minutes and do your sitting, start to finish. Day one hundred and sixteen.

howItsDone: A daily sitting can take this shape: a bell or clear start, an upright posture, a breath practice, and a closing wish of loving-kindness or dedication of merit.

original.note: Pali: the cross-legged sitting posture named in the breathing discourse.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation takes an hour and a cushion.
what it means: a simple, repeatable sitting with a shape: bell, posture, breath, metta.
what a scholar hears: MN 118 describes sitting pallankam abhujitva, folding the legs crosswise, with the body set upright; closing with metta or a sharing of merit is a later custom.
